articleTitle: Second International Conference on Road Traffic Monitoring (Conf. Publ. No.299)
publicationTitle: Second International Conference on Road Traffic Monitoring, 1989.

articleTitle: TITAN: a traffic measurement system using image processing techniques
publicationTitle: Second International Conference on Road Traffic Monitoring, 1989.
abstract: Presents the vehicle detection algorithms which have been developed using the traffic images collected from various scenes covering 100-250 m of a three three-lanes freeway. Pictures can be of front or rear views. The algorithms cope with the possibility of using remote controlled cameras. This means that the system includes features which are able to re-calibrate the algorithms and to detect the lanes if an operator has moved the camera. Different luminance and traffic conditions are considered. Emphases are made upon the new 'lane detection' module and analysis of dense traffic and nocturnal traffic.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Microprocessor and PC-based vehicle classification equipments using induction loops
publicationTitle: Second International Conference on Road Traffic Monitoring, 1989.
abstract: The Laboratory of Traffic and Transportation Engineering of the Helsinki University of Technology (HUT) has developed and built up already three generations of traffic analysers for field research needs. All these equipments have in common that they use induction loop technique to detect the traffic and microprocessors to process the signals given by the detectors. The paper summarises some of the experience gained on building and using these traffic analysers. It deals with general principles and aspects of traffic flow research. The hardware and software of the analysers, especially the latest and most advanced one, are described.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Automatic vehicle recognition
publicationTitle: Second International Conference on Road Traffic Monitoring, 1989.
abstract: Describes a process to classify vehicles into simple groups, in real time, using TV pictures as an input source. The image processing is done using RAPAC, a special purpose image processing machine developed at the University of Sheffield.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Image processing system using cameras for vehicle surveillance
publicationTitle: Second International Conference on Road Traffic Monitoring, 1989.
abstract: The Metropolitan Expressway Public Corporation (MEPC) installed a computer-based traffic control system in 1973 and has revised the system in 1985. This new system processes the data from vehicle detectors and renews information on 400 variable message signs automatically in every minute. The maximum time lag is three minutes. Closed circuit television (CCTV) cameras are installed to survey the complex traffic condition at main points and at intervals of about one kilometer. Five different type of image processing equipment from different manufacturing companies were installed and tested. The purpose of the experiment was to confirm the performance, accuracy, and feature of each equipment and to investigate their adaptability and problems to the traffic control systems.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Road traffic monitoring using the TRIP II system
publicationTitle: Second International Conference on Road Traffic Monitoring, 1989.
abstract: Traffic observed by video cameras or captured on video tape can now be counted automatically in real-time. The aim of the TRIP II system is to take full advantage of the area sensing capability of video images. It is different from many earlier systems since it is based upon an inexpensive IBM AT microcomputer and can processes complex pattern information by simulating the operation of a neural network. In this particular case the vehicle detection algorithm relies on the ability of the TRIP II system to learn from example and discriminate between complex patterns within video images of traffic scenes.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Queue detection using computer image processing
publicationTitle: Second International Conference on Road Traffic Monitoring, 1989.
abstract: The use of a computer to monitor camera images and draw an operators attention to a particular scene when an abnormality in traffic behaviour is detected would have considerable utility. The aim of this research is to develop an algorithm whereby some description, albeit qualitative, of the current traffic state over the image could be obtained directly from image data. An analysis of the effect of camera position has been carried out to determine over what range such a system could be expected to work and to offer some guidance as to the best camera position.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Camera and computer-aided traffic sensor
publicationTitle: Second International Conference on Road Traffic Monitoring, 1989.
abstract: Devlonics Control NV has developed, in co-operation with the Belgian Government and Leuven University, an advanced technology road traffic detection, measurement and control system, known as CCATS. CCATS uses video camera sensors coupled to electronic units that undertake image signal processing in numeric mode. CCATS units are now going into operational service in Europe. The system provides complete and accurate data on road traffic conditions and automatic traffic control. Particularly significant in CCATS development has been the software means to differentiate between wanted data from video images of moving vehicles and unwanted information from moving shadows, reflections, rain, hail, snow etc.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Automatic traffic data collection using aerial video images
publicationTitle: Second International Conference on Road Traffic Monitoring, 1989.
abstract: Aerial video observation of traffic can be evaluated automatically under certain conditions. The method developed at the University of Karlsruhe allows automatic calculation of a wide range of traffic parameters, e.g. speed distribution functions, densities or overtakings. The time-space-trajectories of vehicles can be estimated. The data set describes traffic in the most general form and can be used for determination of traffic conditions, interactions between vehicles, analysis of influences on traffic flow and other (specialized) investigations.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Evaluation of video-recognition equipment for number-plate matching
publicationTitle: Second International Conference on Road Traffic Monitoring, 1989.
abstract: Describes how a number-plate recogniser unit (NRU), developed by Computer Recognition Systems Ltd., has been evaluated for transport planning purposes. Topics covered include a detailed statistical analysis of the error rates associated with the different number-plate syntaxes and character sets currently in use, under a wide variety of conditions. In order to generate number-plates on a computer, a video camera and image processing equipment was used to capture an image of the whole alphabet for each font. This was then subdivided into sections corresponding to individual characters, which could then be redisplayed as required to form a number-plate.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: No stop electronic toll payment systems
publicationTitle: Second International Conference on Road Traffic Monitoring, 1989.
abstract: The topics described include: toll stations and toll rings in Norway; no stop lanes in toll stations; no stop electronic toll payment systems; the Philips PREMID system; and the 'KOFRI' microwave communication system.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Low energy microwave automatic communications system (LEMACS)
publicationTitle: Second International Conference on Road Traffic Monitoring, 1989.
abstract: The Communications Research Group (CRG) of Newcastle Polytechnic and the Transport Operations Research Group (TORG) of the University of Newcastle upon Tyne have been collaborating on the development of a microwave data-communications system between moving vehicle and a roadside beacon, since the end of 1985. A continuation of this work is the development of a two-way communications system which has been designed to satisfy the requirements of nonstop toll collection. It is intended to investigate its potential for use in other road traffic information applications. The high data rates make this system suitable for applications such as the transmission of drive information and route guidance.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: A telemetric monitoring and analysis system for use during large scale population evacuations
publicationTitle: Second International Conference on Road Traffic Monitoring, 1989.
abstract: Describes the on-going development of an operational, prototype real-time traffic monitoring and analysis system (RTMAS) whose purpose is to record and warn of the build-up of significant urban population evacuations in times of threat. In tracking an evacuation build-up, RTMAS is being developed to collect and cumulate net traffic movements (i.e. net regional outflows), building up a quantitative picture of the timing and directions of an evacuation. This is information not currently available in any other form, other than data obtained from very small, and increasingly expensive, post-evacuation household interviews.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Automatic monitoring of traffic conditions by re-identification of vehicles
publicationTitle: Second International Conference on Road Traffic Monitoring, 1989.
abstract: Due to economic and ecological restraints there is an increasing demand for traffic monitoring and control systems in order to operate road traffic within the existing road network more efficiently. The basis for such systems is the knowledge of the actual traffic condition within the whole network; a traffic data acquisition system is required to deliver this information automatically, reliably and in real-time to authorities and drivers. A system called MAVE is introduced which uses pattern recognition principles and correlation methods to measure the so-called section-related traffic data such as journey speed and traffic density. The system works completely passively, i.e. it does not require additional on-board devices for vehicles, therefore an identification of individual drivers is not possible.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Dynamic axle and vehicle weight measurements
publicationTitle: Second International Conference on Road Traffic Monitoring, 1989.
abstract: A trial of high speed weigh-in-motion (WIM) equipment was conducted by the Transport and Road Research Laboratory in February 1987. This trial provided information on the measurement accuracy of several commercial and research equipments for a range of axle weights and heavy goods vehicle categories. The paper reports the trial and provides summarized results obtained from the five research and commercial organisations that took part. Brief descriptions are given of the equipment, (including a capacitive pad transducer, a strain gauge and piezoelectric transducers) calibration procedures, environmental conditions and data analysis methods.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Traffic monitoring and information technology: the case of the Perugia urban freeway
publicationTitle: Second International Conference on Road Traffic Monitoring, 1989.
abstract: The Perugia urban freeway is a four-lane by-pass with six exits, approximately 11 kilometres long, a large part of which consists of viaducts and tunnels. The Umbrian regional authorities requested the Department of Transport to carry out a study prior to installing a computerized traffic-monitoring system, which should be operational by the end of the 1980s. The paper examines: the functions performed by the system; the software necessary for its management; and the architecture and components of the system.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Monitoring traffic in the whole motorway network: what effects can be expected?
publicationTitle: Second International Conference on Road Traffic Monitoring, 1989.
abstract: The author looks at the traffic broadcasting scheme for motorways. It is necessary to search for solutions which allow motorists to select only relevant messages and which allow broadcasters to continue a good program alongside a traffic message system. A possible solution which can be realized in the near future is the transmission of digitally encoded traffic messages via the radio-data-system (RDS). The so-called traffic message channel (TMC) of DRS makes it possible to continuously transmit traffic messages without disturbing the radio programme.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Traffic counts and classifications: distributed data processing
publicationTitle: Second International Conference on Road Traffic Monitoring, 1989.
abstract: Describes a series of electronic data processing systems called MASTRA which is being developed by the Danish Road Directorate. MASTRA handles data from road traffic counts and classifications, and the systems are used by both the local and the national road authorities. MASTRA is a distributed system consisting of a central database for the entire country (placed at the Road Data laboratory) and several PC-systems are fitted according to the demands of different kinds of users. Each user has a PC-system which can work independently of the central system.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Traffic control at a strategic level
publicationTitle: Second International Conference on Road Traffic Monitoring, 1989.
abstract: The paper is concerned with the coordination of traffic control measures on major trunk routes and motorways, but the principles outlined should generally apply to urban networks also. A coordinated strategic control system would require to continually monitor the behaviour of traffic at key points. Parallel systems would provide details of weather conditions, special events, availability of emergency services, roadworks, etc. This data would be held in a real time database. The important feature of the coordinated strategic control system is that the incident response plan is able to take prompt action to minimise the effect of an incident by structured changes to the sub-systems providing the traffic control.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Washington State's high tech approach data to data collection analysis (road traffic)
publicationTitle: Second International Conference on Road Traffic Monitoring, 1989.
abstract: The severe reduction in personnel, and consequently the funds, resulted in a desperate search for more productive methods. The key thrust, of course, was to automate the activities and conserve human resources wherever possible. The balance of the paper describes what the office has accomplished to date and what is under consideration for the near future.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Autowarn-a motorway incident detection and signalling system
publicationTitle: Second International Conference on Road Traffic Monitoring, 1989.
abstract: A system known as Autowarn has been developed by the Department of Transport's Traffic Control and Communication Division with the assistance of software consultants F.I. Group. This system is installed on the M4 motorway and its objective is to protect traffic approaching the Severn Bridge from the east. The presence and clearance of obstructions is detected by monitoring occupancy and smoothed speed traffic parameters. The paper describes Autowarn, how it was evaluated, and the results of the evaluation.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Road traffic monitoring in Hong Kong
publicationTitle: Second International Conference on Road Traffic Monitoring, 1989.
abstract: Describes how the Annual Traffic Census is conducted, the resources involved and how the methodology and techniques may be developed in the future. The field data collected from the automatic counters and manual counts are subject to initial checks for inconsistencies by comparison with the previous results at the same station. The data are then fed into microcomputers (IBM compatible XT/AT type) for further checking and analysis using the purpose design programs (a suite of 12 subprograms written in FORTRAN) to provide the following output: traffic flow variations (monthly, daily and hourly) and characteristics; annual average daily traffic (AADT) and annual growth; vehicle classification and occupancy; vehicle flow and passenger movements across cordons and screenlines; and estimated overall vehicle kilometrage in the territory.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Concepts for vehicle route guidance
publicationTitle: Second International Conference on Road Traffic Monitoring, 1989.
abstract: Developments in information technology has progressed to a point where vehicles can communicate with a complex infrastructure to provide benefits to the vehicle drivers and road traffic authorities. One of the first applications will be the introduction of vehicle route guidance. A common European system architecture is required which will encompass the needs of various countries, drivers and vehicle types. This would provide an architecture on which other information and safety systems could be developed. The paper describes the results of a research study into possible system architectures for vehicle route guidance.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: SCOOT data and route guidance
publicationTitle: Second International Conference on Road Traffic Monitoring, 1989.
abstract: The SCOOT urban traffic control system has been designed to improve traffic control by calculating and implementing optimum signal timings to give minimum overall network delay. a key feature of SCOOT is its traffic model which predicts the main elements of traffic performance-such as flow, delay stops and congestion-from information received every second from detectors on each link in the network. In addition to its use for network control, this up-to-the-minute information is available for any other purpose and can be obtained via standard SCOOT messages at a variety of levels of detail. The paper describes the characteristics and accuracy of the data available from SCOOT which could be useful for route guidance and discusses possible ways in which the data may be used for this purpose.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Traffic data collection-automation of the national core census and the incorporation of dynamic axle weighing
publicationTitle: Second International Conference on Road Traffic Monitoring, 1989.
abstract: The Department of Transport's core census has been operative since 1979 and is a vehicle classification census used to predict trends in national traffic. The Department is in the process of automating this census by installing vehicle classification equipment at 100 sites in England and Wales; an additional 20 sites are being installed in Scotland by the Scottish Development Department. The classified data is collected automatically by a central computer. The paper describes the equipment used to classify and retrieve the data, the progress to date, the further development of the equipment and the future incorporation of dynamic axle weighing for which initial trials of weighing systems have been carried out.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: New sensors for axle detection and weigh-in-motion
publicationTitle: Second International Conference on Road Traffic Monitoring, 1989.
abstract: New axle sensors based on piezoelectric plastic and piezoresistive elastomer have recently become available. The paper describes laboratory and field tests conducted to characterise the new sensors and to determine their suitability for use in axle detection and in weigh-in-motion (WIM).<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: The application of interactive video disc technology to the Norwegian national road network
publicationTitle: Second International Conference on Road Traffic Monitoring, 1989.
abstract: 3M have developed the interactive highway management workstation which consists of a modified SUN 160 workstation, two video disc players, a high resolution colour video monitor and mouse. The software is written in INGRES and 'C' and includes a specially developed screen driver to allow video input to be mixed and displayed with text and graphics generated by the SUNOS operating system. The workstation allows the highway engineer to view map photographs at each of the various scales. The maps can be traversed until the area of the network of interest is displayed. Zooming in and out can be achieved by selecting different photographs using mouse and cursor.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Automatic vehicle identification for non-stop toll collection-the Virginia experience
publicationTitle: Second International Conference on Road Traffic Monitoring, 1989.
abstract: Summarizes progress on a major US project to automate toll collection on the Dulles toll road in Virginia, using automatic vehicle identification (AVI) technology. The Dulles Toll Road AVI-based 'Fastoll' equipment is part of an integrated system which also includes conventional cash toll collection. It will bring substantial benefits in terms of time and cost savings, increased convenience and reduced congestion to commuters from Northern Virginia into Washington DC.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Estimating traffic flows-a new approach to an old problem
publicationTitle: Second International Conference on Road Traffic Monitoring, 1989.
abstract: Highways are there to carry traffic. Information on the volume of traffic carried is an important aspect of the data held in a highway information system. The traffic flow estimation methods described are being tested using the data collected for the traffic monitoring programmes in Somerset and Dorset. The results have been very encouraging and the work will suggest ways in which the methods may be used to optimise counting strategy.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Detection of road hazards-problems and practicalities
publicationTitle: Second International Conference on Road Traffic Monitoring, 1989.
abstract: The prevention of avoidable accidents and the management of traffic during any incident have been a focus of attention in recent years. The paper considers the means of detecting hazardous conditions and the use of one particular algorithm HIOCC, to develop and install a practical incident detection system in the United Kingdom. The method utilises single site detection and the occupancy parameter from road loop detection. This algorithm was tested at seven sites on the M1 in Bedfordshire and carefully assessed.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Automatic vehicle identification for heavy vehicle monitoring
publicationTitle: Second International Conference on Road Traffic Monitoring, 1989.
abstract: Describes the current status of research and development efforts into automatic vehicle identification being undertaken as part of the US Heavy Vehicle Electronic Licence Plate (HELP) programme. The programme is aimed at investigating and developing an integrated heavy vehicle monitoring and management system, combining automatic vehicle identification (AVI), weigh-in-motion and automatic vehicle classification technologies with a networked data communications and processing system, comprising roadside stations linked to regional and central computers. The paper concentrates on the development of an AVI system specification for HELP.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Traffic monitoring in Great Britain
publicationTitle: Second International Conference on Road Traffic Monitoring, 1989.
abstract: Describes briefly the Department of Transport's present system of traffic data collection in Britain, and considers how it is hoped to develop the system in the future both to improve the accuracy of the estimates to provide improved services to their customers. The main 'customers' are those sections of the Department involved in the planning and maintenance of the road system, and in the monitoring of road accidents. The main effort is, therefore, designed to provide estimates of traffic by type of road and by type of vehicle for Great Britain as a whole.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Traffic survey system in Hungary
publicationTitle: Second International Conference on Road Traffic Monitoring, 1989.
abstract: In Hungary, a unified system of traffic surveys has been developed gradually, the elements of which are as follows: general traffic census of the national road system; general traffic census of the local road system; monitoring traffic flows on the national road system; continuous observation of traffic volumes at border crossing points; country-wide origin-destination survey; and other regular or ad-hoc surveys. Changes in the survey methods are characterised by two main tendencies: improving data collection and processing methods; and increasing the compatibility of different survey types.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Method of measuring travel time by using ultrasonic vehicle profile classifiers
publicationTitle: Second International Conference on Road Traffic Monitoring, 1989.
abstract: As an approach to develop an effective real-time prediction system, a new system has been developed to measure the time used by vehicles to travel a certain section of a road. The system identifies special vehicles at the entrance and the exit of the section with ultrasonic vehicle classifiers. The first field experiment was made in 1986 at a section of 500 m length on the route 17 in Saitama Prefecture, and proved that the system was capable of measuring travel time. Further tests were conducted in 1987 and 1988 at the 1 to 3 km long sections of the route 17, and the maximum length of section applicable to the system was also studied. The conclusion of the tests was that the mean time for travelling a section of up to 2 km length has been obtained by using the system. Essentials of the tests are reported.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Integrated automatic vehicle location and position reporting system
publicationTitle: Second International Conference on Road Traffic Monitoring, 1989.
abstract: There is a positive requirement for centralised displays in the fleet operations room. The paper describes an integrated automatic vehicle location and position reporting system which fulfils this requirement. The system can be subdivided into three main sub-systems although these are integrated and interdependent: navigation, position reporting, and data gathering and display. The system philosophy pays great attention to the need to operate continuously without breaks, this is achieved by a high level of redundancy with hot standby capabilities.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: A capacitative strip sensor for measuring dynamic type forces
publicationTitle: Second International Conference on Road Traffic Monitoring, 1989.
abstract: A novel capacitative strip sensor for measuring moving dynamic wheel forces has been designed, developed, and tested. The principle features of the sensor are linear response, insensitivity to loading width and pressure, and static calibration. The design of the sensor and the operation of the signal processing are described. The theoretical performance of the sensor is considered, and the results of full-scale tests using an instrumented lorry are presented.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Autoguide-electronic route guidance for London and the UK
publicationTitle: Second International Conference on Road Traffic Monitoring, 1989.
abstract: Autoguide is the name given to in-vehicle route guidance systems in the UK which are dynamic, i.e. they respond to traffic conditions in calculating recommended routes. Such systems depend upon an infrastructure of roadside beacons. The paper describes the Autoguide system design, and outlines the objectives for the proposed pilot system. It discusses the importance of the emerging draft standard on road-vehicle communication and looks forward to widespread European availability of compatible dynamic route guidance systems. It also discusses in particular the opportunities offered by Autoguide in traffic monitoring.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: The automation of toll-collection and road-use pricing systems
publicationTitle: Second International Conference on Road Traffic Monitoring, 1989.
abstract: Following recent experiments in Hong Kong on road-use pricing, and in Berlin and London on route-guidance, it is clear the technological advance in the fields of data-communications and road traffic 'informatics' (RTI) will reopen the longstanding debate as to how use of the road system should be charged for. In particular, if vehicles can be charged for road-use automatically, without stopping them to do so, then policy towards road-use pricing could be significantly changed, although the strong social and political objections may still remain to be overcome. The paper is not just centred on the technical issues posed by automatic toll-collection but clearly set within the social/political context surrounding any widespread implementation of such a policy.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>
